sections.model_projection: The model projects Chicago Bears 23.26, Carolina Panthers 21.93, for a Bears margin of 1.33 points. The projected total is 45.18. The market currently has Carolina as a 3-point home favorite, meaning the model leans 1.67 points toward Chicago relative to that line.
sections.offensive_matchup: Chicago's offense grades out significantly better than Carolina's, posting an offensive EPA per play of +0.085 (7th) versus Carolina's -0.084 (26th). The Bears also convert at a 46.3% offensive success rate (10th) compared to Carolina's 41.5% (25th), meaning Chicago generates positive expected-points plays far more consistently. Carolina's defense allows a 46.2% opponent success rate (21st), so it does not offer much resistance to a Bears offense that already operates at an above-average efficiency level. Carolina's offense, meanwhile, faces a Bears defense that sits at a middling 18th in defensive EPA per play, leaving some room for the Panthers to move the ball but not enough to overcome the efficiency gap.
sections.quarterback_edge: Caleb Williams carries a career EPA per dropback of 0.00 across 1,229 career attempts, while Bryce Young sits at -0.145 over 1,431 attempts — a meaningful gap that is the second-largest single contributor to Chicago's model edge, worth 0.77 points toward the Bears. Williams also averages 6.6 yards per attempt versus Young's 5.98. sections.trenches: The trench battle is split but decisive in Chicago's favor overall. Carolina's offensive line grades as the stronger unit in pass protection relative to Chicago's pass rush, producing a positive edge score for the Panthers there. However, Chicago's defensive front is the single biggest model driver, contributing -0.81 points toward Carolina; the Bears' run-defense line-yards-allowed rank of 31st (3.25 line yards per rush) is a concern, but their run-blocking line yards of 3.19 (4th) and the Panthers' run-defense line yards allowed of 3.06 (26th) mean Chicago's ground game should find creases. Carolina's defensive pressure rate without a blitz ranks 30th at 8.7%, meaning the Panthers struggle to generate heat with a base front, which benefits Williams behind an offensive line that ranks 1st in sack rate allowed at 3.4%.
sections.explosive_play_edge: Chicago generates explosive plays (10-plus rushing or 20-plus passing yards) at a 9.8% rate (9th), while Carolina allows them at a 7.8% rate (9th), creating a relatively neutral matchup on that side. Going the other direction, Carolina's offense produces explosives at only a 7.9% rate (22nd) against a Bears defense that allows them at a 10.5% rate (28th), which is the one area where the Panthers could catch up. The net edge favors Chicago by a modest margin, contributing -0.10 points toward Carolina in the model.
sections.third_down_red_zone: Chicago converts third downs at a 43.6% rate (6th) and faces a Carolina defense that allows conversions at a 46.2% rate (30th), a stark mismatch that is the third-largest edge category in the model at -3 edge score. Carolina converts only 36.7% of its own third downs (25th) against a Bears defense that holds opponents to 40.5% (16th), compounding the Panthers' difficulty sustaining drives. In the red zone, Chicago scores touchdowns on 63.4% of trips (13th) while Carolina allows touchdowns on 54.3% of red-zone visits (8th), so the Panthers' red-zone defense is actually a relative strength. Carolina's own red-zone offense converts at only 54.2% (23rd), and the Bears allow touchdowns on 67.3% of opponent red-zone trips (29th), so both teams should score when they get inside the 20.

sections.expected_game_script: Chicago figures to control the pace early, operating with the most plays per game in the league at 66.1 (1st) and the 4th-fastest snap tempo at 29.8 seconds per play, while Carolina runs a slower 31.7-second pace (23rd). The Bears' superior third-down efficiency should allow them to sustain drives and keep Carolina's offense off the field, which matters because the Panthers convert only 36.7% of third downs. Williams should have time to operate behind an offensive line that ranks 1st in sack rate allowed, and he will likely lean heavily on play-action — Chicago uses it at a 32.1% rate (2nd) — against a Carolina defense that generates pressure without a blitz at only an 8.7% rate (30th). Carolina's best path back into the game runs through its own red-zone defense, which holds opponents to a 54.3% touchdown rate (8th), and through the Bears' porous explosive-play defense, where a few chunk plays could keep the Panthers within striking distance. The total of 45.18 projected by the model sits slightly below the market's 46.5, consistent with a game where both offenses face meaningful defensive resistance despite the red-zone vulnerabilities on each side. Expect Chicago to hold a modest lead through most of the game, with Carolina's home-field advantage (worth 1.5 points in the model) keeping the Panthers competitive into the fourth quarter.
